claim: Lupus erythematosus is characterized by photosensitivity, where even ambient ultraviolet radiation exposure can lead to development of inflammatory skin lesions.
source: The autoimmune disease lupus erythematosus (lupus) is characterized by photosensitivity, where even ambient ultraviolet radiation (UVR) exposure can lead to development of inflammatory skin lesions.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical characteristic of lupus supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Langerhans cells limit keratinocyte apoptosis and photosensitivity via ADAM17-mediated release of EGFR ligands.
source: We have previously shown that Langerhans cells (LCs) limit keratinocyte apoptosis and photosensitivity via a disintegrin and metalloprotease 17 (ADAM17)-mediated release of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) ligands and that LC ADAM17 sheddase activity is reduced in lupus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Shipman et al., 2018).

claim: LC ADAM17 sheddase activity is reduced in lupus.
source: We have previously shown that Langerhans cells (LCs) limit keratinocyte apoptosis and photosensitivity via a disintegrin and metalloprotease 17 (ADAM17)-mediated release of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) ligands and that LC ADAM17 sheddase activity is reduced in lupus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Non-lesional skin across human lupus and three murine models (MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, and imiquimod mice) share an IFN-rich environment.
source: We show through transcriptomic analysis a shared IFN-rich environment in non-lesional skin across human lupus and three murine models: MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, and imiquimod (IMQ) mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic data presented in the manuscript (Figures 1-4).

claim: IFN-I inhibits LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in murine and human LCs.
source: IFN-I inhibits LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in murine and human LCs, and IFNAR blockade in lupus model mice restores LC ADAM17 sheddase activity, all without consistent effects on LC ADAM17 protein expression or LC numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: IFNAR blockade in lupus model mice restores LC ADAM17 sheddase activity without consistent effects on LC ADAM17 protein expression or LC numbers.
source: IFN-I inhibits LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in murine and human LCs, and IFNAR blockade in lupus model mice restores LC ADAM17 sheddase activity, all without consistent effects on LC ADAM17 protein expression or LC numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: Anti-IFNAR-mediated LC ADAM17 sheddase function restoration is associated with reduced photosensitive responses that are dependent on EGFR signaling and LC ADAM17.
source: Anti-IFNAR-mediated LC ADAM17 sheddase function restoration is associated with reduced photosensitive responses that are dependent on EGFR signaling and LC ADAM17.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: UVR-induced LC ROS production is reduced in lupus model mice.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) is a known mediator of ADAM17 activity; we show that UVR-induced LC ROS production is reduced in lupus model mice, restored by anti-IFNAR, and is cytoplasmic in origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Anti-IFNAR restores UVR-induced LC ROS production in lupus model mice.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) is a known mediator of ADAM17 activity; we show that UVR-induced LC ROS production is reduced in lupus model mice, restored by anti-IFNAR, and is cytoplasmic in origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: UVR-induced LC ROS is cytoplasmic in origin.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) is a known mediator of ADAM17 activity; we show that UVR-induced LC ROS production is reduced in lupus model mice, restored by anti-IFNAR, and is cytoplasmic in origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: IFN-I promotes photosensitivity at least in part by inhibiting UVR-induced LC ADAM17 sheddase function.
source: Our findings suggest that IFN-I promotes photosensitivity at least in part by inhibiting UVR-induced LC ADAM17 sheddase function and raise the possibility that anifrolumab ameliorates lupus skin disease in part by restoring this function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Anifrolumab may ameliorate lupus skin disease in part by restoring LC ADAM17 sheddase function.
source: Our findings suggest that IFN-I promotes photosensitivity at least in part by inhibiting UVR-induced LC ADAM17 sheddase function and raise the possibility that anifrolumab ameliorates lupus skin disease in part by restoring this function.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings with anti-IFNAR treatment.

claim: Photosensitive skin responses in SLE patients can be associated with worsening systemic autoimmunity and end organ damage.
source: In patients with the systemic form of the disease (SLE), with or without diagnosed cutaneous lupus (CLE), photosensitive skin responses can also be associated with worsening systemic autoimmunity and end organ damage.
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Photosensitive skin inflammation and lifestyle modifications contribute to reduced quality of life in lupus patients.
source: Photosensitive skin inflammation, the accompanying risk of systemic disease flares, and the lifestyle modifications such as sun avoidance needed to prevent UVR-induced skin inflammation all contribute to reduced quality of life (Bachen et al., 2009; Foering et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Two distinct photosensitive SLE mouse models showed a reduction in LC Adam17 mRNA in non-lesional skin which corresponded to reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase activity.
source: Two distinct photosensitive SLE mouse models showed a reduction in LC Adam17 mRNA in non-lesional skin which corresponded to reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase activity, and we could reduce photosensitivity by circumventing the reduced EGFR ligand shedding with topical EGFR ligand application.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Shipman et al., 2018).

claim: Topical EGFR ligand application reduced photosensitivity in SLE mouse models.
source: Two distinct photosensitive SLE mouse models showed a reduction in LC Adam17 mRNA in non-lesional skin which corresponded to reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase activity, and we could reduce photosensitivity by circumventing the reduced EGFR ligand shedding with topical EGFR ligand application.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Shipman et al., 2018).

claim: Non-lesional skin of SLE patients showed reduced epidermal EGFR phosphorylation.
source: Non-lesional skin of SLE patients showed reduced epidermal EGFR phosphorylation and a subset had reduced LC numbers, suggesting that reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function, LC ADAM17 expression and/or LC numbers could potentially contribute to pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Shipman et al., 2018).

claim: A subset of SLE patients had reduced LC numbers in non-lesional skin.
source: Non-lesional skin of SLE patients showed reduced epidermal EGFR phosphorylation and a subset had reduced LC numbers, suggesting that reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function, LC ADAM17 expression and/or LC numbers could potentially contribute to pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Shipman et al., 2018).

claim: A prominent interferon signature indicative of exposure to type I interferon is found in tissues and circulating cells in lupus.
source: A prominent interferon (IFN) signature indicative of exposure to type I interferon (IFN-I) is found in tissues and circulating cells in lupus (Baechler et al., 2003; Bennett et al., 2003; Catalina et al., 2019; Der et al., 2019; Jabbari et al., 2014; Kirou et al., 2004; Martínez et al., 2022; Psarras et al., 2020; Psarras et al., 2022), and the recent FDA approval of anifrolumab (anti-IFNAR1) for SLE highlights the importance of IFN-I in disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The recent FDA approval of anifrolumab for SLE highlights the importance of IFN-I in disease pathogenesis.
source: A prominent interferon (IFN) signature indicative of exposure to type I interferon (IFN-I) is found in tissues and circulating cells in lupus (Baechler et al., 2003; Bennett et al., 2003; Catalina et al., 2019; Der et al., 2019; Jabbari et al., 2014; Kirou et al., 2004; Martínez et al., 2022; Psarras et al., 2020; Psarras et al., 2022), and the recent FDA approval of anifrolumab (anti-IFNAR1) for SLE highlights the importance of IFN-I in disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory approval and its implications.

claim: An IFN-I-rich environment is present in even non-lesional skin based on transcriptomic signatures of skin from SLE and CLE patients.
source: Numerous studies have pointed to an IFN-I-rich environment in even non-lesional skin based on transcriptomic signatures of skin from SLE and CLE patients (Billi et al., 2022; Der et al., 2017; Der et al., 2019; Psarras et al., 2020), upregulation of keratinocyte IFN-κ expression in keratinocytes of CLE, SLE, and ANA +patients (Psarras et al., 2020; Stannard et al., 2017), and upregulation of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as MX1 on tissue sections in SLE, incomplete SLE, and ANA +patients (Lambers et al., 2019; Psarras et al., 2020; Reefman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Keratinocyte IFN-κ expression is upregulated in CLE, SLE, and ANA+ patients.
source: Numerous studies have pointed to an IFN-I-rich environment in even non-lesional skin based on transcriptomic signatures of skin from SLE and CLE patients (Billi et al., 2022; Der et al., 2017; Der et al., 2019; Psarras et al., 2020), upregulation of keratinocyte IFN-κ expression in keratinocytes of CLE, SLE, and ANA +patients (Psarras et al., 2020; Stannard et al., 2017), and upregulation of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as MX1 on tissue sections in SLE, incomplete SLE, and ANA +patients (Lambers et al., 2019; Psarras et al., 2020; Reefman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: IFN-stimulated genes such as MX1 are upregulated on tissue sections in SLE, incomplete SLE, and ANA+ patients.
source: Numerous studies have pointed to an IFN-I-rich environment in even non-lesional skin based on transcriptomic signatures of skin from SLE and CLE patients (Billi et al., 2022; Der et al., 2017; Der et al., 2019; Psarras et al., 2020), upregulation of keratinocyte IFN-κ expression in keratinocytes of CLE, SLE, and ANA +patients (Psarras et al., 2020; Stannard et al., 2017), and upregulation of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as MX1 on tissue sections in SLE, incomplete SLE, and ANA +patients (Lambers et al., 2019; Psarras et al., 2020; Reefman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The IFN signature in both lesional and non-lesional skin is greatly enriched compared to the signature in blood.
source: Remarkably, the IFN signature in both lesional and non-lesional skin is greatly enriched compared to the signature in blood (Psarras et al., 2020), further pointing to a potential pathogenic role for IFN-I in lupus skin disease, and the IFN-I-rich environment in grossly unaffected skin points to a role for IFN-I in potentially predisposing to lesion development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Reduced skin lesions in IFNAR-deficient SLE model mice is consistent with a pathogenic role for IFN-I in lupus skin disease.
source: Functionally, the reduced skin lesions in IFNAR-deficient SLE model mice (Nickerson et al., 2013) is consistent with this idea, and, indeed, anifrolmab is especially efficacious for skin disease in SLE patients (Furie et al., 2017; Merrill et al., 2018; Morand et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Anifrolumab is especially efficacious for skin disease in SLE patients.
source: Functionally, the reduced skin lesions in IFNAR-deficient SLE model mice (Nickerson et al., 2013) is consistent with this idea, and, indeed, anifrolmab is especially efficacious for skin disease in SLE patients (Furie et al., 2017; Merrill et al., 2018; Morand et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical studies.

claim: The gene expression profile of non-lesional DLE skin was significantly different from that of healthy skin.
source: The gene expression profile of the non-lesional DLE skin was significantly different from that of healthy skin (Supplementary file 1), lesional skin, and psoriatic skin (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: IFN, IFN-I and IFN-γ pathways were among the upregulated pathways in non-lesional DLE skin compared to normal controls.
source: Differential pathway analysis via Quantitative Set Analysis for Gene Expression (QuSAGE) showed that IFN, IFN-I and IFN-γ pathways were among the upregulated pathways in non-lesional DLE skin compared to normal controls (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by QuSAGE pathway analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The IFN-I pathway was more prominent than the IFNg pathway in non-lesional DLE skin.
source: The IFN-I pathway was more prominent than the IFNg pathway, with upregulation of a number of IFN-I-associated transcription factors such as IRF1, 6, 7, 8 and IFN-stimulated genes including MX1, MX2, XAF1, IFI27, and ISG15 in non-lesional skin (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFN-I-associated transcription factors such as IRF1, 6, 7, 8 are upregulated in non-lesional DLE skin.
source: The IFN-I pathway was more prominent than the IFNg pathway, with upregulation of a number of IFN-I-associated transcription factors such as IRF1, 6, 7, 8 and IFN-stimulated genes including MX1, MX2, XAF1, IFI27, and ISG15 in non-lesional skin (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFN-stimulated genes including MX1, MX2, XAF1, IFI27, and ISG15 are upregulated in non-lesional DLE skin.
source: The IFN-I pathway was more prominent than the IFNg pathway, with upregulation of a number of IFN-I-associated transcription factors such as IRF1, 6, 7, 8 and IFN-stimulated genes including MX1, MX2, XAF1, IFI27, and ISG15 in non-lesional skin (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IFN response was overall less dramatic in non-lesional skin compared to lesional skin.
source: Comparison of non-lesional skin with lesional skin showed that this IFN response was overall less dramatic in non-lesional skin (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with findings of previous studies (Billi et al., 2022; Martínez et al., 2022; Psarras et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citations to previous studies.

claim: ADAR, IRF6, and PTPN1 were expressed at higher levels in non-lesional skin compared to lesional skin.
source: The more muted response did not apply to every gene in the pathway, however, with ADAR, IRF6, and PTPN1 expressed at higher levels in non-lesional skin (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and suggesting a distinct biology in non-lesional and lesional skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Non-lesional and lesional skin have distinct biology.
source: The more muted response did not apply to every gene in the pathway, however, with ADAR, IRF6, and PTPN1 expressed at higher levels in non-lesional skin (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and suggesting a distinct biology in non-lesional and lesional skin.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential gene expression patterns between non-lesional and lesional skin.

claim: Lesional DLE samples were enriched for immune cell gene sets including plasma cells, T cells, monocyte/myeloid cells, neutrophils, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells when compared to controls.
source: Reanalysis of the lesional skin here reiterated the GSVA results of multiple datasets (Martínez et al., 2022), showing enrichment of immune cell gene sets including plasma cells, T cells, monocyte/myeloid cells, neutrophils, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) when compared to controls (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The LC gene set was de-enriched in lesional DLE skin.
source: The LC gene set was de-enriched in lesional skin, echoing the LC loss seen in other studies (Billi et al., 2022; Bos et al., 1986; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982), and this effect was more dramatic than the LC de-enrichment in lesional psoriatic skin (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E and citations to previous studies.

claim: LC de-enrichment in lesional DLE skin was more dramatic than the LC de-enrichment in lesional psoriatic skin.
source: The LC gene set was de-enriched in lesional skin, echoing the LC loss seen in other studies (Billi et al., 2022; Bos et al., 1986; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982), and this effect was more dramatic than the LC de-enrichment in lesional psoriatic skin (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Lesional DLE samples were enriched for inflammatory cytokine gene sets, including IL12, IL21, IL23, TNF, and a highly upregulated IFN gene signature.
source: Lesional DLE samples were also enriched for inflammatory cytokine gene sets, including IL12, IL21, IL23, TNF, and a highly upregulated IFN gene signature as previously seen (Figure 1E; Martínez et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E and citation to previous work.

claim: The upregulation of IFN response genes in lesional DLE skin extended to gene signatures indicative of response to specific IFNs, including IFN-Is (IFN-α, β, κ, and ω) and type II IFNs (IFN-γ).
source: The upregulation of IFN response genes in lesional DLE skin extended to gene signatures indicative of response to specific IFNs, including IFN-Is (IFN-α, β, κ, and ω) and type II IFNs (IFN-γ; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The IFN-γ signature in lesional DLE skin is consistent with the Th1 signature identified in the original study.
source: The IFN-γ signature is consistent with the Th1 signature identified in the original study examining these gene expression data along with cellular phenotyping (Jabbari et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original study.

claim: Non-lesional DLE skin showed upregulation of the IFN gene set when compared to healthy controls, although this change was more modest than in lesional skin.
source: Non-lesional skin also showed upregulation of the IFN gene set in GSVA when compared to healthy controls, although this change was more modest than in lesional skin (Figure 1E–G), similar to that seen in the QuSAGE analysis (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 1E-G.

claim: IFN gene set changes in non-lesional DLE skin were driven by IFN-α, IFN-κ, and IFN-ω gene set upregulation.
source: IFN gene set changes in non-lesional skin were driven by IFN-α, IFN-κ, and IFN-ω gene set upregulation (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Non-lesional DLE skin showed de-enrichment of the LC gene set, and this effect was more modest than in lesional skin.
source: Non-lesional skin showed de-enrichment of the LC gene set and this effect was more modest than in lesional skin (Figure 1E and G), consistent with the noticeable loss of LCs in lesional skin compared to adjacent non-lesional skin by immunostaining of tissue sections (Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 1E and G, and citation to previous work.

claim: Non-lesional DLE skin showed de-enrichment of the keratinocyte gene set, an effect not seen in lesional skin.
source: In contrast, non-lesional skin showed de-enrichment of the keratinocyte gene set, an effect not seen in lesional skin (Figure 1E and G), suggesting a distinct biology in non-lesional and lesional skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 1E and G.

claim: The MRL/lpr model has a Fas gene mutation and develops a lupus-like phenotype especially well on the MRL genetic background.
source: The photosensitive MRL/lpr model has a Fas gene mutation and develops a lupus-like phenotype especially well on the MRL genetic background (Menke et al., 2008; Theofilopoulos and Dixon, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: MRL/lpr mice have reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function and LC Adam17 mRNA.
source: MRL/lpr mice have reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function and LC Adam17 mRNA, and topical EGFR ligand supplementation ameliorated photosensitivity (Shipman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Topical EGFR ligand supplementation ameliorated photosensitivity in MRL/lpr mice.
source: MRL/lpr mice have reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function and LC Adam17 mRNA, and topical EGFR ligand supplementation ameliorated photosensitivity (Shipman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The IFN-α/β and IFN-γ pathways were among the most highly expressed in MRL/lpr mice compared to control MRL/+ mice.
source: QuSAGE pathway analysis showed that the IFN-α/β and IFN-γ pathways were among the most highly expressed in MRL/lpr mice compared to control MRL/+mice (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by QuSAGE pathway analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: IRF 1, 2, 7, and 9 transcription factors and a number of their targets were expressed at higher levels in MRL/lpr mice.
source: Consistent with the activation of IFN pathways, IRF 1, 2, 7, and 9 transcription factors and a number of their targets were expressed at higher levels in MRL/lpr mice (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The B6.Sle1yaa lupus model is driven by the Sle1 lupus susceptibility locus derived from lupus-prone NZB2410 mice in combination with the Y chromosome autoimmune accelerator locus whose effects are attributed to Tlr7 duplication.
source: The B6.Sle1yaa lupus model is driven by the Sle1 lupus susceptibility locus derived from lupus-prone NZB2410 mice in combination with the Y chromosome autoimmune accelerator locus whose effects are attributed to Tlr7 duplication (Pisitkun et al., 2006; Subramanian et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: B6.Sle1yaa mice are photosensitive and have reduced LC Adam17 mRNA expression.
source: B6.Sle1yaa mice are photosensitive and have reduced LC Adam17 mRNA expression (Shipman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: B6.Sle1yaa mice expressed elevated levels of several lupus related genes from the Yaa locus including Tlr7.
source: As expected, compared to B6 controls, B6.Sle1yaa mice expressed elevated levels of several lupus related genes from the Yaa locus including Tlr7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Several genes involved in the regulation of and response to IFN were expressed at higher levels in B6.Sle1yaa mice, including Irf7, Irf9, Isg15, Xaf1, Selp, and Ube2l6.
source: Although differences between the B6 and B6.Sle1yaa transcriptomes were modest (Figure 2E; Supplementary file 6), several genes involved in the regulation of and response to IFN were expressed at higher levels, including Irf7, Irf9, Isg15, Xaf1, Selp, and Ube2l6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: LC numbers as a proportion of total cells were not different in B6.Sle1yaa mice at 10 months of age when this model is fully diseased.
source: LC numbers as a proportion of total cells were not different at 10 months of age when this model is fully diseased (Shipman et al., 2018), but Cd207 expression was downregulated in these younger (5 month old) diseased mice when compared to B6 controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), potentially hinting at either reduced LC numbers at this time point or altered CD207 expression on LCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cd207 expression was downregulated in 5 month old B6.Sle1yaa mice when compared to B6 controls.
source: LC numbers as a proportion of total cells were not different at 10 months of age when this model is fully diseased (Shipman et al., 2018), but Cd207 expression was downregulated in these younger (5 month old) diseased mice when compared to B6 controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), potentially hinting at either reduced LC numbers at this time point or altered CD207 expression on LCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The IMQ model is induced by 4–5 weeks of topical IMQ, a TLR 7/8 agonist, resulting in autoantibody production, enlarged spleen and lymph nodes, nephritis, and photosensitivity characteristic of SLE.
source: The IMQ model is induced by 4–5 weeks of topical IMQ, a TLR 7/8 agonist, resulting in autoantibody production, enlarged spleen and lymph nodes, nephritis, and photosensitivity characteristic of SLE (Ambler et al., 2022; Goel et al., 2020; Yokogawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The contralateral ear in IMQ mice demonstrated an IFN-I signature, with upregulation of a number of ISGs and IRF 7 and 9.
source: Similar to non-lesional skin in the MRL/lpr mice, the contralateral ear in IMQ mice demonstrated an IFN-I signature, with upregulation of a number of ISGs and IRF 7 and 9 (Figure 2F–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 7, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 2F-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IFN gamma pathways were not upregulated in IMQ mice, in contrast to MRL/lpr mice.
source: In contrast to MRL/lpr mice, IFN gamma pathways were not upregulated in IMQ mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of pathway analysis results between MRL/lpr and IMQ mice.

claim: MRL/lpr mice showed increased enrichment of a number of inflammatory cell and cytokine gene sets including T cells, myeloid cells, neutrophils, pDCs, IFN, IL1, IL21, and TNF.
source: By GSVA using lupus-relevant murine gene sets (Supplementary file 9), MRL/lpr mice showed increased enrichment of a number of inflammatory cell and cytokine gene sets including T cells, myeloid cells, neutrophils, pDCs, IFN, IL1, IL21, and TNF (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The keratinocyte signature was enriched in MRL/lpr mice, in contrast to the de-enrichment of this gene set in human DLE.
source: The keratinocyte signature was enriched in MRL/lpr mice, in contrast to the de-enrichment of this gene set in human DLE (Figure 1G, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 1G and 3A.

claim: The LC signature did not show any quantitative changes in MRL/lpr mice, consistent with unchanged LC numbers in the skin of MRL/lpr mice.
source: The LC signature did not show any quantitative changes; assuming that this gene set could in part reflect LC numbers, this result was consistent with unchanged LC numbers in the skin of MRL/lpr mice (Shipman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis and citation to previous work.

claim: The IFN gene set upregulation in MRL/lpr non-lesional skin was broad, with significant enrichment of gene signatures induced by stimulation from multiple IFNs.
source: Similar to human DLE, the IFN gene set upregulation in MRL/lpr non-lesional skin was broad, with significant enrichment of gene signatures induced by stimulation from multiple IFNs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: B6.Sle1yaa mice showed upregulation of the IFN gene set without a particular contribution from any one IFN.
source: B6.Sle1yaa mice showed less dramatic differences than the MRL/lpr model, but also showed upregulation of the IFN gene set without a particular contribution from any one IFN (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figures 3C-D.

claim: The LC gene set was de-enriched in B6.Sle1yaa mice.
source: The LC gene set was de-enriched in B6.Sle1yaa mice (Figure 3C), driven in part by the reduction in Cd207 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), potentially reflecting decreased LC numbers or altered LC phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3C and gene expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The contralateral 'non-lesional' ears from IMQ-treated mice exhibited significant upregulation of the IFN gene signature and were similar to MRL/lpr mice in showing enriched gene signatures of myeloid cells, IL21, and TNF.
source: The contralateral 'non-lesional' ears from IMQ-treated mice also exhibited significant upregulation of the IFN gene signature and were similar to MRL/lpr mice in showing enriched gene signatures of myeloid cells, IL21, and TNF (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: T cell genes were uniquely de-enriched in IMQ skin.
source: T cell genes were uniquely de-enriched in IMQ skin (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The LC gene set was not altered in non-lesional IMQ skin.
source: The LC gene set was not altered (Figure 3E), although there was de-enrichment in IMQ-painted ipsilateral skin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IFN signature in non-lesional IMQ skin reflected enrichment of multiple IFN-I gene sets.
source: Similar to human DLE and MRL/lpr mice, the IFN signature in non-lesional IMQ skin reflected enrichment of multiple IFN-I gene sets (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The overall IFN gene set was not enriched in the IMQ-painted ipsilateral skin.
source: Interestingly, the overall IFN gene set was not enriched in the IMQ-painted ipsilateral skin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although there was enrichment in two of the specific IFN signatures (IFNB1 and IFNW1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: All genes common to human DLE, MRL/lpr, and IMQ datasets (Sprr1b, Isg15, Ddx60, Bst2, Xaf1, Rsad2, Slc7a8, Ifit3) were interferon-inducible genes.
source: All of these genes (Sprr1b, Isg15, Ddx60, Bst2, Xaf1, Rsad2, Slc7a8, Ifit3) were interferon-inducible genes.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of overlapping differentially expressed genes shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In pairwise set overlaps (DLE – MRL/lpr, MRL/lpr – IMQ or IMQ – MRL/lpr) large proportion of overlapping genes were IFN-inducible targets including Ifi genes (Ifi44, 203, 204), IRF transcription factors (Irf 1,2,7, 8, and 9), Oas 2,3 and L2, Mx1.
source: Similarly, in pairwise set overlaps (DLE – MRL/lpr, MRL/lpr – IMQ or IMQ – MRL/lpr) large proportion of overlapping genes were IFN-inducible targets including Ifi genes (Ifi44, 203, 204), IRF transcription factors (Irf 1,2,7, 8, and 9), Oas 2,3 and L2, Mx1 (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of overlapping differentially expressed genes.

claim: IFN upregulation correlated with loss of LCs in human DLE and B6.Sle1yaa mice but not in MRL/lpr and IMQ mice.
source: Notably, IFN upregulation correlated with loss of LCs in human DLE and B6.Sle1yaa mice but not in MRL/lpr and IMQ mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of GSVA scores shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The lack of correlation between IFN upregulation and LC loss in IMQ mice extended to the painted ipsilateral ear, where there was a reduced LC signature in the absence of IFN upregulation.
source: The lack of correlation in IMQ mice also extended to the painted ipsilateral ear, where there was a reduced LC signature in the absence of IFN upregulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: UVR treatment of a mixture of digested epidermal cells induced LC cell surface TNFR1 loss.
source: As we had studied LC ADAM17 sheddase activity using isolated LCs, we confirmed here that UVR treatment of a mixture of digested epidermal cells also induced LC cell surface TNFR1 loss (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: UVR-induced LC cell surface TNFR1 loss is LC ADAM17-dependent.
source: This effect was LC ADAM17-dependent (Figure 5A), validating UVR-induced LC cell surface TNFR1 loss as a readout of LC ADAM17 activity in the context of a mixture of epidermal cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A comparing WT and LCAd17 mice.

claim: IFN-κ reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase activity by nearly 40% when used to treat LCs ex vivo.
source: IFN-κ, an IFN-I that is highly expressed by lupus keratinocytes (Tsoi et al., 2019), reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase activity by nearly 40% when used to treat LCs ex vivo (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IFN-κ reduced LC ADAM17 protein levels only modestly by 8% and had no effect on cell viability.
source: In contrast, IFN-κ reduced LC ADAM17 protein levels only modestly by 8% and had no effect on cell viability (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D-E.

claim: The IFN-κ-driven inhibition of ADAM17 activity was abrogated by the JAK1/3 inhibitor tofacitinib.
source: The IFN-κ-driven inhibition of ADAM17 activity was abrogated by the JAK1/3 inhibitor tofacitinib (Figure 5F) without altering ADAM17 protein levels (Figure 5G) or cell viability (Figure 5H), supporting the idea that IFN-κ mainly affected LC ADAM17 by inhibiting sheddase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5F-H.

claim: IFN-β reduced LC ADAM17 activity without effects on cell viability ex vivo.
source: Another IFN-I, IFN-β, similarly reduced LC ADAM17 activity without effects on cell viability ex vivo (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5I-J.

claim: In vivo application of IFN-κ to the skin of wildtype B6 mice reduced LC ADAM17-mediated shedding by 57%.
source: In vivo, application of IFN-κ to the skin of wildtype B6 mice reduced LC ADAM17-mediated shedding by 57% (Figure 5K) while cell surface ADAM17 was reduced by 9% (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5K-L.

claim: In vivo application of IFN-κ to the skin of wildtype B6 mice reduced cell surface ADAM17 by 9%.
source: In vivo, application of IFN-κ to the skin of wildtype B6 mice reduced LC ADAM17-mediated shedding by 57% (Figure 5K) while cell surface ADAM17 was reduced by 9% (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: In vivo application of IFN-κ had no effect on LC numbers.
source: There was no effect on LC numbers (Figure 5M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: IFN-β reduced human LC ADAM17 activity by 62% without altering ADAM17 expression or LC viability.
source: Addition of IFN-β reduced LC ADAM17 activity by 62% without altering ADAM17 expression or LC viability (Figure 5N–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5N-P.

claim: MRL/lpr mice showed a 42% reduction in LC ADAM17 sheddase activity when compared to control MRL/+ mice.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Shipman et al., 2018), MRL/lpr mice showed a 42% reduction in LC ADAM17 sheddase activity when compared to control MRL/+mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: LC ADAM17 protein levels in MRL/lpr mice showed a 21% reduction compared to controls.
source: LC ADAM17 protein levels, however, were less affected, showing a 21% reduction (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Intraperitoneal anti-IFNAR treatment of MRL/lpr mice at 500 μg/dose restored UVR-induced LC TNFR1 loss.
source: Intraperitoneal (i.p.) anti-IFNAR treatment of MRL/lpr mice at 500 μg/dose restored UVR-induced LC TNFR1 loss (Figure 6A), suggesting restoration of LC ADAM17 sheddase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Anti-IFNAR at 500 μg/dose did not alter cell surface ADAM17 protein expression in MRL/lpr mice.
source: Anti-IFNAR did not alter cell surface ADAM17 protein expression (Figure 6B), suggesting that IFN-I regulated LC ADAM17 sheddase function rather than expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A lower 125 μg/dose of anti-IFNAR had similar effects in restoring LC ADAM17 sheddase activity without affecting LC ADAM17 protein levels in MRL/lpr mice.
source: A lower 125 μg/dose of anti-IFNAR had similar effects in restoring LC ADAM17 sheddase activity without affecting LC ADAM17 protein levels (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: LCs from the B6.Sle1yaa model showed a 63% reduction in UVR-induced TNFR1 loss when compared to control B6 mice without a corresponding change in cell surface ADAM17 protein levels.
source: LCs from the B6.Sle1yaa model showed a 63% reduction in UVR-induced TNFR1 loss when compared to control B6 mice without a corresponding change in cell surface ADAM17 protein levels (Figure 6E–F), suggesting reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function in this SLE model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6E-F.

claim: Anti-IFNAR restored LC ADAM17 activity in B6.Sle1yaa mice without increasing ADAM17 protein expression.
source: Similar to MRL/lpr mice, anti-IFNAR restored LC ADAM17 activity in B6.Sle1yaa mice without increasing ADAM17 protein expression (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6E-F.

claim: IMQ model mice showed reduced UVR-induced TNFR1 loss without alterations in cell surface ADAM17 protein levels when compared to controls.
source: Similar to the B6.Sle1yaa model, IMQ model mice showed reduced UVR-induced TNFR1 loss without alterations in cell surface ADAM17 protein levels when compared to controls (Figure 6G–H), suggesting reduced LC ADAM17 sheddase function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6G-H.

claim: LC numbers were unchanged from controls in the IMQ model.
source: Similar to the MRL/lpr and B6.Sle1yaa models (Shipman et al., 2018) and consistent with the unchanged LC gene set by GSVA (Figure 3E), LC numbers were unchanged from controls in the IMQ model (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Anti-IFNAR restored LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in IMQ mice and did not alter LC numbers.
source: Anti-IFNAR restored LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in IMQ mice and did not alter LC numbers (Figure 6G,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6G and 6I.

claim: LC ADAM17 sheddase activity was consistently reduced across three lupus models examined.
source: While LC ADAM17 protein levels were not consistently affected and LC numbers were unchanged in the three lupus models examined, LC ADAM17 sheddase activity was consistently reduced (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on summary of data presented in Table 1.

claim: Manipulation of IFNAR signaling in lupus models consistently regulated only LC ADAM17 sheddase activity.
source: Furthermore, manipulation of IFNAR signaling in these models, similar to treating human and murine LCs with IFN-I, consistently regulated only LC ADAM17 sheddase activity (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on summary of data presented in Table 1.

claim: Anti-IFNAR treatment at 500 μg/dose reduced ear swelling in MRL/lpr mice.
source: Anti-IFNAR treatment at 500 μg/dose reduced ear swelling in MRL/lpr mice (Figure 7A–B) but did not reduce epidermal permeability, a readout of skin barrier function (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A-B.

claim: Anti-IFNAR treatment at 500 μg/dose did not reduce epidermal permeability in MRL/lpr mice.
source: Anti-IFNAR treatment at 500 μg/dose reduced ear swelling in MRL/lpr mice (Figure 7A–B) but did not reduce epidermal permeability, a readout of skin barrier function (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In control MRL/+ mice, anti-IFNAR at 500 μg/dose increased UVR-induced ear swelling and epidermal permeability.
source: Surprisingly, in control MRL/+mice, anti-IFNAR actually increased UVR-induced ear swelling and epidermal permeability (Figure 7B–C), suggesting that anti-IFNAR at this dose-induced photosensitivity in non-lupus mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7B-C.

claim: IFNAR deficiency in non-lupus B6 mice induced photosensitivity.
source: These results echoed findings by other groups that IFNAR deficiency in non-lupus B6 mice induced photosensitivity (Sontheimer et al., 2017) and reduced skin wound healing (Gregorio et al., 2010; Wolf et al., 2022), and we considered the possibility that the 500 μg anti-IFNAR dose perhaps mimicked complete IFNAR deficiency and disrupted normal skin functions, thus obscuring the effects of LC ADAM17 activity restoration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: IFNAR deficiency reduced skin wound healing in non-lupus B6 mice.
source: These results echoed findings by other groups that IFNAR deficiency in non-lupus B6 mice induced photosensitivity (Sontheimer et al., 2017) and reduced skin wound healing (Gregorio et al., 2010; Wolf et al., 2022), and we considered the possibility that the 500 μg anti-IFNAR dose perhaps mimicked complete IFNAR deficiency and disrupted normal skin functions, thus obscuring the effects of LC ADAM17 activity restoration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Reducing anti-IFNAR to 125 μg/dose still increased UVR-induced MRL/+ ear swelling but no longer increased epidermal permeability.
source: Reducing anti-IFNAR to 125 μg/dose still increased UVR-induced MRL/+ear swelling but no longer increased epidermal permeability (Figure 7D–E), suggesting a decreased pathologic effect on physiologic skin functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D-E.

claim: Anti-IFNAR at 125 μg/dose was sufficient to reduce both UVR-induced skin swelling and epidermal permeability in MRL/lpr mice.
source: This lower dose, which was sufficient to restore LC ADAM17 activity in MRL/lpr mice (Figure 6C), was sufficient to reduce both UVR-induced skin swelling and epidermal permeability (Figure 7D–E) and limit neutrophil and monocyte infiltration after UVR exposure (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D-E.

claim: Anti-IFNAR at 125 μg/dose limited neutrophil and monocyte infiltration after UVR exposure in MRL/lpr mice.
source: This lower dose, which was sufficient to restore LC ADAM17 activity in MRL/lpr mice (Figure 6C), was sufficient to reduce both UVR-induced skin swelling and epidermal permeability (Figure 7D–E) and limit neutrophil and monocyte infiltration after UVR exposure (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The small molecule EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor PD168393 abrogated the anti-IFNAR-mediated reduction in ear swelling and epidermal permeability in MRL/lpr mice.
source: The small molecule EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor PD168393 (PD16) abrogated the anti-IFNAR-mediated reduction in ear swelling and epidermal permeability (Figure 7H–I), suggesting that anti-IFNAR requires EGFR signaling to ameliorate photosensitivity in MRL/lpr mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7H-I.

claim: IMQ mice were characterized by monocyte accumulation while neutrophils were lower in number.
source: IMQ mice were characterized by monocyte accumulation while neutrophils were lower in number (Figure 7J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7J-K.

claim: Anti-IFNAR reduced the monocyte cell infiltrate in UVR-treated skin of IMQ mice and had no effect on neutrophil numbers.
source: Anti-IFNAR reduced the monocyte cell infiltrate in UVR-treated skin and had no effect on neutrophil numbers (Figure 7K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Anti-IFNAR had no effect on LC numbers in IMQ mice.
source: LC numbers were unaffected (Figure 7L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: In IMQ-treated LCAd17 mice lacking ADAM17 in LCs, anti-IFNAR failed to reduce monocyte accumulation.
source: In IMQ-treated LCAd17 mice lacking ADAM17 in LCs (Shipman et al., 2018), however, anti-IFNAR failed to reduce monocyte accumulation (Figure 7K), suggesting that the ameliorative effects of anti-IFNAR on UVR-induced inflammation are, in part, dependent on LC ADAM17.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: UVR exposure upregulated mainly cytoplasmic ROS in LCs.
source: Assessment of cytoplasmic versus mitochondrial LC ROS showed that UVR exposure upregulated mainly cytoplasmic ROS (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8B-C.

claim: Skin from IMQ-treated mice showed a reduction in UVR-induced LC ROS generation when compared to control skin.
source: Skin from IMQ-treated mice showed a reduction in UVR-induced LC ROS generation when compared to control skin, and anti-IFNAR treatment of IMQ mice restored UVR-driven ROS generation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Anti-IFNAR treatment of IMQ mice restored UVR-driven ROS generation.
source: Skin from IMQ-treated mice showed a reduction in UVR-induced LC ROS generation when compared to control skin, and anti-IFNAR treatment of IMQ mice restored UVR-driven ROS generation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Photosensitivity in the MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, and IMQ lupus models shares pathogenic mechanisms with human lupus.
source: Our results also suggest that photosensitivity in the MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, and IMQ lupus models shares pathogenic mechanisms with human lupus, underscoring the utility of these models for the study of lupus skin pathophysiology.
evidence: This is inferred from the shared IFN signatures and LC dysfunction across human and murine models.

claim: LC ADAM17 sheddase inhibition is a mechanism by which the IFN-rich environment primes non-lesional skin for photosensitive responses.
source: Our data here, and especially the experiments showing the importance of EGFR signaling and LC ADAM17 in the ameliorative effects of anti-IFNAR on photosensitive responses, suggest that LC ADAM17 sheddase inhibition is a mechanism by which the IFN-rich environment primes non-lesional skin for photosensitive responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing anti-IFNAR effects depend on EGFR signaling and LC ADAM17.

claim: Keratinocytes are likely to be an important source of IFN-I that causes LC ADAM17 sheddase dysfunction.
source: Given that LCs are positioned among the suprabasal layer of the epidermis near basal and spinous keratinocytes that demonstrate high IFN expression and signaling (Billi et al., 2022; Psarras et al., 2020; Sarkar et al., 2018), keratinocytes are likely to be an important source of IFN-I that causes LC ADAM17 sheddase dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial relationship between LCs and keratinocytes and the known IFN expression by keratinocytes.

claim: There is a potential pathogenic feed-forward loop between LCs and keratinocytes in lupus skin whereby keratinocyte-derived IFN-I causes LC ADAM17 sheddase dysfunction and this dysfunction contributes to greater UVR-induced keratinocyte damage, skin inflammation, and lesion formation.
source: This possibility coupled with our data here point to a potential pathogenic feed-forward loop between LCs and keratinocytes in lupus skin whereby keratinocyte-derived IFN-I causes LC ADAM17 sheddase dysfunction and this dysfunction contributes to greater UVR-induced keratinocyte damage, skin inflammation, and, over time, lesion formation.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental findings and known biology.

claim: IFNs have distinct functions in non-lesional and lesional skin.
source: Our findings suggest the possibility that IFNs have distinct functions in non-lesional and lesional skin.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of anti-IFNAR in control versus lupus mice and the different IFN signatures in non-lesional versus lesional skin.

claim: Skin upregulates IFN-I with injury and infection, and the IFN is important in part for tissue repair and wound healing.
source: Physiologically, skin upregulates IFN-I with injury and infection, and the IFN is important in part for tissue repair and wound healing (Gregorio et al., 2010; Wolf et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The IFN-I in non-lesional skin in mice and humans reflects a repair response to a mild insult such as immune complex deposition that forms the 'lupus band' found in non-lesional human lupus skin.
source: This may explain why anti-IFNAR treatment of control MRL/+mice with physiologic IFN-I levels increased UVR-induced skin inflammation and suggests that the IFN-I in non-lesional skin in mic and humans reflects a repair response to a mild insult such as immune complex deposition that forms the 'lupus band' found in non-lesional human lupus skin.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The upregulated IFN in non-lesional skin, by causing LC ADAM17 dysfunction or heightened keratinocyte responses, serves to 'prime' the skin for further injury and a second insult such as UVR manifests as a photosensitive response.
source: The upregulated IFN in non-lesional skin, by causing LC ADAM17 dysfunction or heightened keratinocyte responses, serves to 'prime' the skin for further injury and a second insult such as UVR manifests as a photosensitive response (Billi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the experimental data and cited work.

claim: Because the repair response is compromised, IFN signaling continues to be upregulated, further inhibiting repair responses and promoting inflammation, tissue damage processes, and lesion formation.
source: Because the repair response is compromised, IFN signaling continues to be upregulated, further inhibiting repair responses and promoting inflammation, tissue damage processes, and lesion formation.
evidence: This is a speculative model of disease progression.

claim: IFN in non-lesional skin primes for further injury, and the (higher) IFN in lesional skin reflecting frustrated tissue repair, continues to prime but also contributes to tissue damage.
source: In this model, then, IFN in non-lesional skin primes for further injury, and the (higher) IFN in lesional skin reflecting frustrated tissue repair, continues to prime but also contributes to tissue damage.
evidence: This is a speculative model of disease progression.

claim: IFNAR blockade should both prevent new lesion formation and treat existing lesions as long as physiologic IFN levels for wound healing are preserved.
source: IFNAR blockade, then, should both prevent new lesion formation and treat existing lesions as long as physiologic IFN levels for wound healing are preserved.
evidence: This is a therapeutic prediction based on the proposed disease model.

claim: Increased ADAM17 activity can promote inflammation, such as by release of TNF or EGFR ligands within inflamed joints or lupus kidneys.
source: Increased ADAM17 activity can promote inflammation, such as by release of TNF or EGFR ligands within inflamed joints or lupus kidneys (Issuree et al., 2013; Qing et al., 2018); yet loss of ADAM17 can compromise barrier surfaces (Blaydon et al., 2011; Franzke et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Loss of ADAM17 can compromise barrier surfaces.
source: Increased ADAM17 activity can promote inflammation, such as by release of TNF or EGFR ligands within inflamed joints or lupus kidneys (Issuree et al., 2013; Qing et al., 2018); yet loss of ADAM17 can compromise barrier surfaces (Blaydon et al., 2011; Franzke et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: IFN-I reduces LC ROS generation to inhibit ADAM17 function.
source: Here, we identify IFN-I as a negative regulator of LC ADAM17 sheddase function, and our data suggest a scenario whereby IFN-I reduces LC ROS generation to inhibit ADAM17 function.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the experimental data on ROS and ADAM17 activity.

claim: LC ADAM17 sheddase function dysregulation is a key contributor to the propensity for photosensitivity and is thus a therapeutic target.
source: Our data here showing that the regulation of LC ADAM17 sheddase activity by IFN-I is uncoupled from LC ADAM17 protein expression and LC numbers (summarized in Table 1) supports the idea that LC ADAM17 sheddase function dysregulation is a key contributor to the propensity for photosensitivity and is thus a therapeutic target.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent regulation of sheddase activity independent of protein expression and cell numbers.

claim: The uncoupling of ADAM17 sheddase activity from protein expression is consistent with the known biology of ADAM17 on other cell types.
source: The uncoupling of ADAM17 sheddase activity from protein expression is consistent with the known biology of ADAM17 on other cell types, where sheddase function is triggered by many stimuli on other cell types including UVR and G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and controlled by mediators such as ROS and iRhoms, as we and others have shown (Li et al., 2015; Zunke and Rose-John, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The ability to modulate ADAM17 enzymatic function offers the ability to regulate UVR responses in a more timely manner and with a much greater and tunable dynamic range than control of Adam17 transcription and translation or LC numbers.
source: We speculate that the ability to modulate ADAM17 enzymatic function offers the ability to regulate UVR responses in a more timely manner and with a much greater and tunable dynamic range than control of Adam17 transcription and translation or LC numbers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the biological advantages of regulating enzyme activity.

claim: Targeting the effects of IFN-I on LC ADAM17 sheddase function offers the opportunity to have a large impact in protecting the skin and systemic complications.
source: Targeting the effects of IFN-I on LC ADAM17 sheddase function, then, offers the opportunity to have a large impact in protecting the skin and systemic complications.
evidence: This is a therapeutic implication inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: LC loss is a feature of human lupus skin.
source: Our data along with recent reports indicates that LC loss is a feature of human lupus skin (Billi et al., 2022), with the effect being variable in non-lesional skin (Martínez et al., 2022; Shipman et al., 2018; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982; this report) and a greater more consistent effect in lesional skin (Bos et al., 1986; Martínez et al., 2022; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and data from this manuscript.

claim: LC loss is variable in non-lesional human lupus skin.
source: Our data along with recent reports indicates that LC loss is a feature of human lupus skin (Billi et al., 2022), with the effect being variable in non-lesional skin (Martínez et al., 2022; Shipman et al., 2018; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982; this report) and a greater more consistent effect in lesional skin (Bos et al., 1986; Martínez et al., 2022; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and data from this manuscript.

claim: LC loss is greater and more consistent in lesional human lupus skin.
source: Our data along with recent reports indicates that LC loss is a feature of human lupus skin (Billi et al., 2022), with the effect being variable in non-lesional skin (Martínez et al., 2022; Shipman et al., 2018; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982; this report) and a greater more consistent effect in lesional skin (Bos et al., 1986; Martínez et al., 2022; Sontheimer and Bergstresser, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: LC numbers appeared less affected in lupus mouse models compared to human lupus.
source: On the other hand, LC numbers appeared less affected in lupus mouse models, with reduction of the LC signature in the 5-month-old B6.Sle1yaa non-lesional skin and in the IMQ painted ear of IMQ mice, but otherwise with normal LC numbers in non-lesional skin of MRL/lpr, 10-month-old B6.Sle1yaa (Shipman et al., 2018) and IMQ mice (this report).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of LC data across human and murine models.

claim: High IFN-I states are also seen in viral infections, genetic interferonopathies, and other autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis and dermatomyositis.
source: High IFN-I states are also seen in viral infections, genetic interferonopathies, and other autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis and dermatomyositis (Muskardin and Niewold, 2018) in which photosensitivity is found in the former and is a disease hallmark in the latter (Werth et al., 2004; Wysenbeek et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Photosensitivity is found in genetic interferonopathies and is a disease hallmark in dermatomyositis.
source: High IFN-I states are also seen in viral infections, genetic interferonopathies, and other autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis and dermatomyositis (Muskardin and Niewold, 2018) in which photosensitivity is found in the former and is a disease hallmark in the latter (Werth et al., 2004; Wysenbeek et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Autoimmune disease-like manifestations that include photosensitivity are among the immune-related adverse events in cancer patients treated with checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Autoimmune disease-like manifestations that include photosensitivity are among the immune-related adverse events in cancer patients treated with checkpoint inhibitors (Brahmer et al., 2018), a situation where distinct IFN-I-mediated processes may have specific roles in promoting anti-tumor immunity and treatment resistance (Benci et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Distinct IFN-I-mediated processes may have specific roles in promoting anti-tumor immunity and treatment resistance in cancer patients treated with checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Autoimmune disease-like manifestations that include photosensitivity are among the immune-related adverse events in cancer patients treated with checkpoint inhibitors (Brahmer et al., 2018), a situation where distinct IFN-I-mediated processes may have specific roles in promoting anti-tumor immunity and treatment resistance (Benci et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.
